metadata.title: Predictive insights into U.S. students’ mathematics performance on PISA 2022 using ensemble tree-based machine learning models

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for the United States and merges student and school files using the school identifier (CNTSCHID), assigning school-level predictors to students within the same school. The analytic dataset comprises 4,552 students in 154 schools, with outcomes based on the 10 PISA 2022 mathematics plausible values (PV1MATH–PV10MATH). Although the authors discuss sampling weights and cite guidance suggesting weighting may be less critical for ML, they explicitly do not include sampling weights in the analysis. The paper also applies preprocessing steps (dropping predictors with >50% missingness, removing identical/redundant variables, and imputing remaining missing predictor values using missForest), and then splits the data into training (80%) and test (20%) sets before fitting the ML models.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for 15-year-old students in the United States. Merged student and school questionnaires using CNTSCHID so that school-level predictors were assigned to students within the same school. For predictors, removed variables with >50% missing values, removed identical variables (same values for all students), and removed redundant variables (e.g., kept ESCS while excluding the component DVs used to compute ESCS). For the remaining predictors, imputed missing values using missForest (RF-based imputation). The final modeling dataset was split into training (80%, N=3644) and test (20%, N=908).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison using reduced predictor sets: XGBoost (best) rMSE=66.39 with 10 selected predictors; Random Forest rMSE=69.82 with 5 selected predictors; LightGBM rMSE=66.36 with 10 selected predictors. Full-model rMSEs: RF 63.69, XGBoost 60.47, LightGBM 60.43. Efficiency (training time): XGBoost 4.14 s vs LightGBM 22.93 s vs RF 129.27 s. Predictor-selection criterion: ARE threshold 0.1 (reduced model close to full).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data for U.S. 15-year-olds, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-directed learning to predict mathematics achievement (averaged across PV1MATH–PV10MATH), finding that these ML-selected predictors achieved low prediction error with XGBoost (rMSE=66.39) and that XGBoost was the most efficient among the best-accuracy tree ensembles. This indicates that strengthening student self-efficacy and foundational math familiarity—alongside targeted supports linked to socioeconomic resources and learning support at home—may be more actionable than relying solely on literature-driven predictor selection, though the results are predictive (not causal) and do not incorporate sampling weights.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 mathematics performance for U.S. 15-year-old students (n=4,552 in 154 schools) and predicts mathematics achievement using the 10 PVs (PV1MATH–PV10MATH) as separate outcomes, then averages results across PVs. After cleaning predictors (dropping variables with >50% missingness, removing identical and redundant variables) and imputing remaining missing predictor values with missForest, the authors train three ensemble tree models—Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—using 5-fold cross-validation on an 80/20 train/test split. For reduced models selected via an ARE<0.1 criterion, XGBoost achieved rMSE=66.39 (10 predictors) and the lowest training time (4.14 s), outperforming RF (rMSE=69.82; 129.27 s) and matching LightGBM’s accuracy (rMSE=66.36; 22.93 s). The most influential predictors include mathematics self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupation status, and family support for self-directed learning. The paper explicitly omits sampling weights for ML, so estimates may not fully reflect the complex survey design, and the use of ALE supports interpretation but does not establish causality.
